title: Asking with onko with plural owners
summary: Ask with onko and meillä, teillä, and heillä.
objectives: Ask with onko and meillä, teillä, and heillä.
Apply the pattern using the supporting forms shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Ask with onko and meillä, teillä, and heillä.
Add the yes/no question ending -ko to on: on + -ko = onko. Put onko first, then the owner, then one thing in its basic singular form.
keyPoints: Ask with onko and meillä, teillä, and heillä.

steps: Several owners do not require olemmeko. Possession still begins with onko.
meillä means “we as the owner”. Put the owner after onko.
pallo (“ball”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
The group owner teillä does not require oletteko; keep onko.
teillä means “you as the owner” for a group. Put the owner after onko.
kynä (“pen”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
Heillä does not require ovatko. The possession question still uses onko.
heillä means “they as the owner”. Put the owner after onko.
peli (“game”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.
The noun’s front vowels do not change onko to onkö; the question ending attaches to on.
heillä means “they as the owner”. Put the owner after onko.
tyyny (“pillow”) stays in its basic singular form at the end.

commonMistakes: Add -ko to fixed on to form onko; plural owners do not require olemmeko or ovatko.
Keep the noun form shown in the task. This pack models basic singular nouns; partitive questions are also natural in other contexts.

practiceExercises.prompt: Optional practice: Translate “Onko heillä pallo?” into English. Owner: they.
practiceExercises.explanation: The -lla/-llä phrase identifies the owner; onko stays fixed in this possession pattern.

parts.formation: On + the yes/no question ending -ko = onko. It stays the same with every possessor.

parts.formation: he has the learned possession form heillä; its -lla/-llä ending marks the possessor. Learn this pronoun form as a whole.
